title: Judiciary
summary: Supreme Court, High Courts, lower courts, tribunals, and the power of judicial review.

subcards.title: Judiciary: overview
subcards.summary: How India's single court system works, stays independent, and picks its judges.
at_a_glance: Government of India Act 1935 (integrated courts); USA (independence of judiciary)
Made by Supreme Court judgments, not by Constitution text
Created by the 99th Amendment 2014; struck down by the Supreme Court on 16 Oct 2015
Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Parliament does not vote on them)

blocks.text: The judiciary means the courts: the Supreme Court, the High Courts and the lower courts. Their job is to decide disputes, administer justice and protect people's rights.

head: Aspect
India
USA

Integrated (single) — one ladder of courts
Double — federal courts and a separate set of state courts
Which laws a court applies
The same court applies both Central (Union) and State laws
Federal courts apply federal laws; state courts apply state laws
Source

items: Example: on the same day a district judge applies an Act of Parliament in one case and a State Act in the next. This shows the integrated judiciary.
India is a federation like the USA, but unlike the USA it has one unified judiciary and one system of basic law and justice for the whole country.
Exam answer: the Constitution has established an integrated and independent judicial system (not a 'dual', 'plural' or 'partial' one).

blocks.title: National Mission for Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms (2011)
items: Set up by the Union Government (Department of Justice) in August 2011.

Its twin objectives: (1) increasing access to justice by reducing delays and arrears (pending cases) in the system; (2) enhancing accountability through structural changes and by setting performance standards and capacities.
Studying and recommending more judges for the Supreme Court and High Courts is NOT one of its stated objectives.

blocks.text: see Subordinate courts for the district-level hierarchy

Independence of the judiciary means the courts work free from pressure of the executive (the government, that is the Council of Ministers) and the legislature. This idea is taken from the USA Constitution. It is part of the basic structure (the core features that Parliament cannot destroy even by amendment).

blocks.title: Safeguards (Laxmikanth)
head: Safeguard
What it means
rows: Mode of appointment
The President appoints judges only after consulting senior judges, including the Chief Justice of India (CJI). So the government alone cannot choose judges.
Security of tenure
A judge can be removed only on the grounds and by the procedure written in the Constitution. The President cannot remove a judge at will ('at pleasure').
Fixed service conditions

Parliament fixes judges' salary, allowances and pension. After appointment these cannot be changed to the judge's disadvantage. The only exception is a Financial Emergency (Article 360), when the President can reduce them.
Expenses charged on Consolidated Fund of India
Salaries, pensions, staff and office costs are non-votable: Parliament may discuss them but does not vote on them.
Conduct cannot be discussed
Parliament and the State Legislatures cannot discuss a judge's conduct, except when a motion to remove that judge (impeachment motion) is being considered.
Ban on practice after retirement
Retired Supreme Court judges cannot plead (argue cases) in any court or before any authority in India.
Power to punish for contempt
The courts can punish anyone for contempt of court (disrespecting or obstructing the court).
Freedom to appoint staff
The CJI appoints the Supreme Court's officers and staff, without interference from the government.
Jurisdiction cannot be curtailed
Parliament can increase, but cannot reduce, the Supreme Court's jurisdiction (powers to hear cases).
blocks.note: Wrong options seen in exams: 'Supreme Court judges can be removed by the CJI only' is false — the President removes a judge only after an address (a removal motion passed by a special majority) by both Houses of Parliament. 'Staff are appointed by the Government after consulting the CJI' is false — the CJI appoints the staff.

blocks.title: Separation of judiciary from executive
items: Article 50 (a Directive Principle of State Policy, in Part IV): the State shall separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
So this separation comes from a Directive Principle. It is not in the Preamble or the Seventh Schedule, and it is not just a convention (custom).

sections.heading: How judges are appointed: Judges cases

blocks.text: Article 124(2): the President appoints Supreme Court judges after 'consultation' with the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and other judges. Article 217: High Court judges are appointed after consulting the CJI, the Governor of the state and the Chief Justice of that High Court. The President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers, not on the Prime Minister's sole recommendation. The Judges cases below were a fight over one word: what does 'consultation' mean?

blocks.title: The Judges cases
head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: First Judges case — S.P. Gupta (1981; judgment often dated 1982)
'Consultation' does NOT mean 'concurrence' (agreement). It only means exchanging views, so the President need not follow the CJI.
The government (executive) had the final say
Second Judges case — Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (1993)

'Consultation' means 'concurrence'. The CJI's advice binds the President, but the CJI must first take the views of the 2 senior-most Supreme Court judges. Only the senior-most Supreme Court judge should become CJI.
The collegium system was born; judges' opinion got primacy (the upper hand). This overruled S.P. Gupta.
Third Judges case — In re Presidential Reference (1998), an advisory opinion given under Article 143

For Supreme Court appointments the CJI must consult a collegium of the 4 senior-most Supreme Court judges. If 2 of them object, the name should not be recommended. A recommendation made without following these rules does not bind the Government.
The collegium was expanded to the CJI and 4 judges (5 in all)
Fourth Judges case — Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (2015)
The 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act were both struck down
The collegium system was restored

blocks.title: Who the CJI consults (Third Judges case)
head: Decision
CJI consults
rows: Appointment of a Supreme Court judge
4 senior-most Supreme Court judges (a collegium of 5 including the CJI)
Appointment of a High Court judge
2 senior-most Supreme Court judges
Transfer of a High Court judge (Article 222)
4 senior-most Supreme Court judges, and also the views of the Chief Justices of BOTH High Courts (the one the judge leaves and the one the judge goes to)

blocks.title: Collegium and Memorandum of Procedure (MoP)
items: The collegium means judges choosing judges. It is not written in the Constitution; it comes from Supreme Court decisions (the Second and Third Judges cases).
MoP means Memorandum of Procedure: the written procedure for appointing Supreme Court and High Court judges, framed after the 1993 judgment and the 1998 opinion.
For the post of CJI, the MoP says the senior-most Supreme Court judge who is considered fit to hold the office is appointed.

Steps for appointing a CJI: (1) the Union Law Minister asks the outgoing CJI to recommend a successor; (2) the Law Minister puts the recommendation before the Prime Minister; (3) the Prime Minister advises the President; (4) the President appoints. No resolution of Parliament is needed.

blocks.title: Supersession of senior judges for CJI

items.what: The senior-most Supreme Court judge was always made CJI (a convention, that is, a settled practice followed without a written rule)
A.N. Ray (4th in seniority) was made CJI, superseding (jumping over) J.M. Shelat, K.S. Hegde and A.N. Grover
items.detail: The Government was unhappy with their stand in the Kesavananda Bharati (1973) case; all three resigned

items.what: M.H. Beg was made CJI, superseding H.R. Khanna
items.detail: Khanna was the only judge who disagreed (sole dissent) in ADM Jabalpur (1976); he held that the right to life survives even during an Emergency. He resigned.

items.what: Second Judges case: only the senior-most judge is to be made CJI

sections.heading: NJAC and the Fourth Judges case

items: The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act 2014 (which inserted Article 124A) and the NJAC Act 2014 were two separate laws.
Together they replaced the collegium with the National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) for appointing Supreme Court and High Court judges.
The NJAC had 6 members: the CJI (chairperson), the 2 senior-most Supreme Court judges after the CJI, the Union Law Minister, and 2 eminent persons.

On 16 Oct 2015, in the Fourth Judges case (Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association v. Union of India), the Court declared BOTH the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act unconstitutional and void — not just the Act.
Reason: the NJAC gave the government (executive) a role in choosing judges, which harms the independence of the judiciary, a basic-structure feature.
The 5-judge bench decided 4:1. Justice J. Chelameswar alone upheld the NJAC; Justices J.S. Khehar, M.B. Lokur, Kurian Joseph and A.K. Goel struck it down.
Result: the old collegium system came back into force.

head: Amendment (year)
Change
rows: Added Article 31A, Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule (laws placed in the Ninth Schedule were shielded from court challenge)
Allowed one common High Court for two or more states; extended High Courts' jurisdiction to Union Territories
Goa, Daman and Diu included in the Indian Union. This is not about courts; it is listed here because exams pair it with judiciary amendments as a wrong option.

Inserted Article 368(4) and (5) to stop courts from reviewing amendments; Article 226A (High Courts barred from testing the validity of Central laws); an All-India Judicial Service under Article 312; tribunals under Article 323A and Article 323B
Removed Article 226A (gave back the High Courts' power)
Created the NJAC (Article 124A); struck down in 2015

items: All-India Judicial Service: allowed by the 42nd Amendment (Article 312), but NO law has created it so far. It cannot include any post below district judge.
A High Court, under Article 226, can examine whether a constitutional amendment is valid, because judicial review is part of the basic structure.

If the Government or legislators dislike a Supreme Court verdict, they have two options: pass a new law that removes the basis of the verdict, or pass a constitutional amendment. Both can still be reviewed by the courts.

items: A.K. Gopalan: preventive detention (jailing a person to prevent a future offence). Maneka Gandhi: personal liberty. S.R. Bommai: President's Rule. Indra Sawhney: reservations.
PIL, the basic structure doctrine and the ban on handcuffing prisoners are the Supreme Court's own creations; 'exemptions to Fundamental Rights' is not one of them.

items: Integrated judiciary comes from the Government of India Act 1935, NOT the British Constitution.
Independence of judiciary is borrowed from the USA.
Article 50 (a Directive Principle) asks the State to separate the judiciary from the executive.
The collegium comes from Supreme Court judgments, not the Constitution. MoP means Memorandum of Procedure.

First Judges case: consultation does not mean concurrence. Second: it does mean concurrence (CJI with 2 judges). Third: CJI with 4 judges for the Supreme Court (for a High Court appointment: CJI with 2 judges).
NJAC: BOTH the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act were declared void (2015); Justice Chelameswar alone dissented.
Appointing a CJI needs no resolution of Parliament: the Law Minister takes the outgoing CJI's recommendation to the Prime Minister, who advises the President.
All-India Judicial Service: provided for by the 42nd Amendment but never actually created.

blocks.title: Appointment
head: Who
How
rows: Other judges (Art 124(2))

Appointed by the President by a warrant (formal order) under his hand and seal. Before this, consulting the CJI is compulsory; the President may also consult such Supreme Court and High Court judges as he thinks necessary
CJI

Appointed by the President. By convention, the senior-most Supreme Court judge, if considered fit, becomes CJI (this is written in the Memorandum of Procedure, MoP – the government–judiciary rulebook on appointments)
CJI route (MoP)
The outgoing CJI recommends his successor; the Union Law Minister sends it to the Prime Minister; the Prime Minister advises the President; the President appoints
Collegium
The collegium is not mentioned in the Constitution – it was created by Supreme Court judgments (the Judges cases). For details, see the Judiciary overview card

blocks.text: see Judiciary overview – First/Second/Third/Fourth Judges cases, NJAC

blocks.title: Qualifications (Art 124(3))
head: Must be
AND one of these
rows: A citizen of India (no exception – even a distinguished jurist must be a citizen)
(a) a High Court judge for 5 years, OR (b) an advocate of a High Court for 10 years, OR (c) a distinguished jurist (eminent legal scholar) in the President's opinion
blocks.note: No minimum age is prescribed. If a dispute arises about a judge's age, it is decided by the authority and in the manner that Parliament fixes by law (Art 124(2A)).

blocks.title: Oath (Art 124(6); form given in the Third Schedule) – taken before the President or a person appointed by him. The judge swears to:
items: bear true faith and allegiance (loyalty) to the Constitution of India
uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India
perform duties without fear or favour, affection or ill-will (no bias for or against anyone)
uphold the Constitution and the laws

blocks.title: Tenure, pay, after retirement
head: Point
Rule
rows: Tenure
Holds office till age 65 (there is no fixed term of years)
Resignation
By writing a letter to the President
Salary (Art 125)

Fixed by Parliament by law. Salary and other privileges cannot be changed to a judge's disadvantage after appointment – the only exception is a Financial Emergency (under Art 360 the President may then reduce the salaries of Supreme Court and High Court judges)
Charged expenditure

The salaries, allowances and pensions of judges and staff, and all administrative expenses of the Court, are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Art 146(3)). 'Charged' means Parliament can discuss them but does not vote on them
CJI gets ₹2.80 lakh and each other judge ₹2.50 lakh per month; pension is 50% of the last salary
After retirement (Art 124(7))
A retired Supreme Court judge cannot plead (argue cases) or act in ANY court or before any authority in India

blocks.title: Independence safeguards (Laxmikanth)
items: Judges are appointed with the judiciary consulted, not by the government alone
Security of tenure – removal only by the hard Parliament process
Service conditions cannot be changed to a judge's disadvantage after appointment
Expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (not voted)
Judges' conduct cannot be discussed in Parliament (Art 121) or in a State Legislature (Art 211)
Ban on legal practice after retirement
Power to punish anyone for contempt of the Court
The CJI appoints the Court's own staff (Art 146)
Parliament can extend (increase) the Court's jurisdiction, but cannot curtail (cut) it

blocks.text: Grounds (Art 124(4)): only two – 'proved misbehaviour' or 'incapacity' (unable to work, for example due to illness). The Constitution does not define these terms. An unpopular judgment, or disagreeing with other judges, is not a ground. The Constitution does NOT use the word 'impeachment' for judges (it uses it only for the President), though people commonly say 'impeachment of a judge'.

blocks.title: Removal of a Supreme Court judge – Art 124(4) and 124(5), and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968

steps.detail: Signed by at least 100 Lok Sabha members (given to the Speaker), or at least 50 Rajya Sabha members (given to the Chairman)
The Speaker or Chairman may admit or refuse the motion – having enough signatures does not force them to admit it
If admitted, a committee of three investigates: (a) the CJI or a Supreme Court judge, (b) the Chief Justice of a High Court, (c) a distinguished jurist
If the committee finds the judge not guilty, the motion stops there. If it finds misbehaviour or incapacity, the House takes up the motion for voting
The motion must be passed by a majority of the total membership of the House AND by at least two-thirds of the members present and voting
The address (formal request) from both Houses must be presented to the President in the SAME session
The judge is removed only by this order of the President – not by Parliament, the CJI or the Cabinet

blocks.text: Article 121: Parliament cannot discuss how a judge behaved while doing judicial duty, except when it is debating a motion asking the President to remove that judge. Article 211: a State Legislature can never discuss it (there is no such exception). A High Court judge is removed in exactly the same way as a Supreme Court judge.
see High Courts (a High Court judge is removed the same way as a Supreme Court judge)

Soumitra Sen (Calcutta High Court)

The Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 proposed a National Judicial Council (made up of the CJI and senior judges) to receive complaints against Supreme Court and High Court judges and inquire into them; it never became law.

sections.heading: Acting, ad hoc & retired judges; seat & procedure

blocks.title: Temporary judges
head: Article
Who
Key conditions
rows: Art 126 – Acting Chief Justice
A Supreme Court judge appointed by the President
Used when the CJI's office is vacant, or the CJI is absent or unable to do the duties
Art 127 – Ad hoc judge
A High Court judge who is qualified to be a Supreme Court judge

Used only when there is no quorum (not enough permanent judges to hold a session). The CJI appoints him with the President's previous consent, after consulting the Chief Justice of that High Court. The ad hoc judge must give Supreme Court sittings priority over his High Court work, and has all the powers of a Supreme Court judge while attending
Art 128 – Retired judge
A retired Supreme Court judge (or a retired High Court judge qualified to be a Supreme Court judge)

The CJI may request him to sit, with the previous consent of the President AND of that person. His allowances are fixed by the President. While sitting he has the powers of a Supreme Court judge, but he is not otherwise treated as a Supreme Court judge

blocks.title: Seat, rules, staff
head: Article
Rule
rows: Art 130 – Seat
The Court sits in Delhi. The CJI may also choose other place(s), with the President's approval. This is optional – nobody can force it
Art 145(1) – Rules
The Court makes its own rules of practice and procedure, with the President's approval, subject to any law made by Parliament
Cases involving a substantial question of interpreting the Constitution, and Presidential references under Art 143, must be heard by at least 5 judges (called a Constitution Bench)
Judgments are delivered only in open court; cases are decided by majority; a judge who disagrees may write a dissenting judgment
Supreme Court Rules, 2013

Every case is ordinarily heard by a bench of not less than 2 judges nominated by the CJI (a single judge sits only for limited matters, such as in chambers or during vacation). Only an Advocate-on-Record (AoR – an advocate who has passed the Supreme Court's own AoR exam) can file papers and act for a party. Other advocates can appear and argue only when instructed by an AoR or permitted by the Court
Advocates Act, 1961 (section 16)

The Supreme Court or a High Court may designate an advocate as a 'Senior Advocate' (with the advocate's consent), for ability, standing at the Bar or special knowledge of law. A Senior Advocate cannot appear in the Supreme Court without an AoR
Art 146

The CJI (or a judge or officer he directs) appoints the Court's staff. Rules on staff salary, leave and pension need the President's approval. The Court's expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, and fees collected by the Court go into the Consolidated Fund of India

blocks.text: Alladi Krishnaswamy Ayyar said: 'The Supreme Court of India has more powers than any other Supreme Court in any part of the world.' It plays four roles: federal court (settles Centre–State disputes), highest court of appeal, guarantor of Fundamental Rights (FRs), and guardian and final interpreter of the Constitution.

blocks.title: Jurisdictions
head: Type
Article
What it covers
rows: Original (exclusive – only the Supreme Court can hear it)
Art 131

Disputes about a legal right between: the Centre and one or more States; the Centre and some States on one side versus other States; or two or more States. Private persons or companies cannot use it, and purely political questions are not covered. Excluded: disputes from pre-1950 treaties or sanads (these can go only through a reference under Art 143(2)); inter-State river water disputes (a tribunal under Art 262); Finance Commission matters; and certain adjustments of expenses and pensions. First such suit: West Bengal vs Union of India, 1961
Writ (original, but not exclusive – High Courts also issue writs)
Art 32

5 writs – habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto – only to enforce Fundamental Rights. A High Court under Art 226 can issue writs for FRs 'and for any other purpose', so its writ power is wider. Parliament may give the Supreme Court writ powers for other purposes too (Art 139)
Appeal – constitutional cases
Art 132
Any case – civil, criminal or other – if the High Court certifies that it involves a substantial question of interpreting the Constitution (certificate given under Art 134A)
Appeal – civil cases
Art 133

The High Court must certify both: (1) the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance, AND (2) the question needs to be decided by the Supreme Court. The old ₹20,000 money-value condition was removed by the 30th Amendment, 1972
Appeal – criminal cases
Art 134

Appeal lies as of right (automatically) if the High Court (a) on appeal reversed an acquittal and sentenced the accused to death, or (b) took a case from a lower court, tried it, and sentenced the accused to death. In other cases, a High Court certificate is needed. A 1970 Act (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) extends the as-of-right appeal to sentences of life imprisonment or 10 years or more. There is no right of appeal when the High Court acquits
Certificate
Art 134A
The High Court decides whether to give a certificate for appeal, either on its own or on an oral request made right after the judgment, and must decide 'as soon as may be' (as quickly as possible)
Special leave to appeal (SLP)

See the next table

On the President's reference, the Supreme Court inquires into misbehaviour of UPSC or State PSC members (its advice is binding on the President). It also supervises all courts in India

head: Power
Meaning

Contempt
It can punish for contempt of itself (Art 129 and Art 142(2)). In 1991 it ruled it can also punish contempt of High Courts, lower courts and tribunals

blocks.title: Contempt of Courts Act, 1971
head: Point
Detail
rows: Origin
Based on the H.N. Sanyal Committee (set up 1961, report 1963). The Constitution does not define contempt; Parliament makes the law on it
Civil contempt
Wilfully (deliberately) disobeying a judgment, order or writ of a court, or wilfully breaking a promise (undertaking) given to a court
Criminal contempt
Publishing anything or doing any act that scandalises (lowers the authority of) a court, interferes with a pending case, or obstructs the administration of justice
Not contempt
Innocent publication, a fair and accurate report of court proceedings, and fair criticism of a case that has been finally decided
Punishment
Simple imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine up to ₹2,000, or both. No contempt case can be started more than 1 year after the act
Who can start criminal contempt

The Supreme Court may act suo motu (on its own), or on a motion by the Attorney General or Solicitor General; any other person (for example a private citizen) needs the written consent of the Attorney General or the Solicitor General

blocks.title: Review & curative
head: Remedy
Rules
rows: Review petition – Art 137
Must be filed within 30 days, before the same judge(s) who gave the judgment. Grounds: new and important evidence, a mistake clearly visible on the face of the record, or any other sufficient reason
Curative petition

Created by the Supreme Court in Rupa Ashok Hurra vs Ashok Hurra (2002), using its inherent power to reconsider its own judgments. A final Supreme Court judgment cannot be challenged by a fresh writ petition under Art 32. Even after a review petition is dismissed, a curative petition can be filed, but only on narrow grounds: violation of natural justice (for example, the person was not heard), bias of a judge, abuse of the court's process, or to cure a gross miscarriage of justice. It is not a second appeal on the merits

items: Inaugurated on 28 Jan 1950, but came into existence on 26 Jan 1950.
Number of judges is fixed by Parliament by ordinary law: 8 in 1950, 34 in 2019, now 38 including the CJI (2026 Act, as of Nov 2026). A key saying 'CJI + 33' is outdated.
No minimum age; Indian citizenship is compulsory, even for a distinguished jurist.
Removal notice needs 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha signatures; the Speaker may still refuse it; the address must be in the same session; only the President's order removes the judge.
Advisory opinion: given only when the President refers; under 143(1) the Court may refuse, under 143(2) it must answer; the opinion never binds the President.
A retired Supreme Court judge cannot practise anywhere in India; a retired High Court judge can practise in the Supreme Court and in other High Courts (not his own).
Contempt power comes from Art 129 and Art 142 – NOT Art 144 (Art 144 is about authorities helping the Court).
Supreme Court writs are only for Fundamental Rights; High Court writs are for FRs and any other purpose. 'Collegiate jurisdiction' is not a real jurisdiction – a common wrong option.
Curative petition (Rupa Ashok Hurra, 2002) comes only after a review petition is dismissed, on narrow grounds – it is not a second appeal.

subcards.title: High Courts (Art 214–231)
subcards.summary: How High Courts are set up, who their judges are, and what powers they have.
at_a_glance: Articles 214–231, in Part VI of the Constitution (a 'Part' is a chapter-group of Articles)
President, after consulting the Chief Justice of India, the Governor and the Chief Justice of that High Court
Art 226 – High Courts can issue writs (court orders) for Fundamental Rights AND 'for any other purpose' (ordinary legal rights)

items: High Courts began in 1862 at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras under the Indian High Courts Act, 1861 (a British Parliament law); a fourth came at Allahabad in 1866.

Art 214: there shall be a High Court for each State. But the 7th Amendment Act, 1956 lets Parliament set up a COMMON High Court for two or more States (or two or more States and a Union Territory) – Art 231. So NOT every State has a High Court of its own.
How the number grew: 18 High Courts → 21 in 2000 (Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Uttarakhand) → 24 in 2013 (Manipur, Meghalaya, Tripura) → 25 in 2019 (Andhra Pradesh). Still 25 as of Nov 2026.
Only 3 High Courts cover more than one State: Bombay, Gauhati, and Punjab & Haryana.

Union Territories (UTs): only Delhi has its own High Court (since 1966); Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh share one. Other UTs come under nearby State High Courts. Parliament alone, by law, can extend or exclude a High Court's jurisdiction (area of authority) for a UT – Art 230 (inserted by 7th Amendment, 1956). A State Legislature CANNOT do this.

blocks.title: Qualifications (Art 217(2))
items: Must be a citizen of India; AND
Must have held a judicial office in India for 10 years, OR been an advocate of a High Court (or of two or more High Courts one after another) for 10 years.
No minimum age is prescribed.
There is no 'distinguished jurist' route (a jurist is an expert in law; this route exists only for the Supreme Court).

blocks.title: Oath, salary, staff
items: Oath (Art 219): before the Governor of the State, or a person appointed by the Governor.
Strength (Art 216): the President decides the number of judges – the Constitution does not fix it. So the President can increase it as workload grows.

Salary (Art 221): fixed by Parliament by law. It cannot be reduced after appointment, except during a Financial Emergency (Art 360). From 2018: Chief Justice ₹2.50 lakh and other judges ₹2.25 lakh per month.

Salaries, allowances and the High Court's expenses are 'charged' on the Consolidated Fund of the STATE. This means the State Legislature does not vote on them, but it CAN discuss them (Art 203(1)). Pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of INDIA.
Staff (Art 229): appointed by the Chief Justice, or by a judge or officer whom the Chief Justice directs. Rules on the staff's salaries, allowances, leave or pensions need the Governor's approval.

Language (Art 348): proceedings are in English. The Governor, with the President's previous consent, may allow Hindi or the State's official language in High Court proceedings – but NOT in judgments, decrees and orders, which stay in English.

sections.heading: Tenure, removal, transfer, and acting/additional/retired judges

blocks.title: Tenure (Art 217)
items: Holds office till 62 years (raised from 60 by the 15th Amendment Act, 1963).
If there is a doubt about a judge's age, the President decides it after consulting the Chief Justice of India; the President's decision is final.
A judge resigns by writing a letter to the President.
A judge leaves office when appointed to the Supreme Court or when transferred to another High Court.

blocks.title: Removal
items: A High Court judge is removed in the same way and on the same grounds as a Supreme Court judge (Art 218 read with Art 124(4)): only for 'proved misbehaviour' or 'incapacity'.

The President orders removal after BOTH Houses of Parliament pass an address (a formal request), each by a special majority (a majority of the total membership AND two-thirds of members present and voting), in the SAME session. The State Legislature has no role.
The procedure is laid down in the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. No High Court judge has been removed (impeached) so far.

Art 121 (for Parliament) and Art 211 (for the State Legislature) bar discussion of a judge's conduct in doing official duties. Only Art 121 has an exception: Parliament may discuss it while considering a removal motion.

blocks.text: see Supreme Court for the full removal procedure

blocks.title: Transfer (Art 222)
items: The President transfers a judge from one High Court to another after consulting the Chief Justice of India. The transferred judge gets a compensatory allowance (extra payment) fixed by Parliament.

1977 case: a transfer should be made only as an exception, in public interest, and not as a punishment. 1994 case: a transfer can be challenged in court (judicial review), but only by the judge who was transferred.

Third Judges case (1998): for a transfer, the Chief Justice of India consults the 4 senior-most Supreme Court judges AND the Chief Justices of BOTH High Courts (the one the judge leaves and the one he joins).

blocks.title: Acting, additional and retired judges
head: Article
Who
Key rules
rows: Acting Chief Justice
The President appoints one of the other judges of that High Court when the Chief Justice's post is vacant, or when the Chief Justice is absent or unable to work
Additional judge
The President appoints when there is a temporary increase in work or arrears (backlog of pending cases); for at most 2 years
Acting judge
Appointed when a judge (other than the Chief Justice) is absent or unable to work, or is acting as Chief Justice; holds office until the permanent judge returns
Age limit
Additional and acting judges cannot continue after age 62, even if their appointment order has time left
Retired judge

The Chief Justice of a High Court may request a retired judge of that or any High Court to sit as a judge. This needs the previous consent of the PRESIDENT and of the retired judge. The retired judge gets allowances fixed by the President and has all the powers of a High Court judge, but is not otherwise treated as a judge of that High Court

sections.heading: Jurisdiction and powers of a High Court

head: Jurisdiction
What it means
Key facts
rows: Original
Hears a case for the first time, not as an appeal

Election disputes of MPs and MLAs (election petitions); revenue matters; enforcement of Fundamental Rights; cases transferred from lower courts that involve a constitutional question (Art 228). The Calcutta, Bombay, Madras and Delhi High Courts also hear high-value civil cases directly
Writ (Art 226)
Can issue 5 writs (court orders): habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto

For Fundamental Rights AND 'for any other purpose' (ordinary legal rights) – so it is WIDER than the Supreme Court's power under Art 32. A High Court can issue a writ to a person or authority outside its territory if the cause of action (the facts that give rise to the case) arises wholly or partly within its territory (added by the 15th Amendment, 1963). This power is shared with the Supreme Court (concurrent). Art 226 itself is NOT a Fundamental Right (Art 32 is)
Appellate
Hears appeals from lower courts

Civil: first appeals (on law and facts), second appeals (on law only), and intra-court appeals (from a single judge to a bench of the same High Court). Criminal (under the BNSS – Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023): if convicted after a trial by a Sessions Judge or Additional Sessions Judge, the appeal goes to the High Court; if convicted after a trial by a Magistrate (for example a Chief Judicial Magistrate), the appeal goes to the Court of Session. A death sentence given by a Sessions Court must be confirmed by the High Court, whether or not there is an appeal
Supervisory (Art 227)
Supervises (superintendence) all courts and tribunals in its territory

Does NOT cover courts or tribunals set up under armed-forces laws. It may call for reports (returns) from lower courts, make rules, prescribe forms and fix fees – but these rules must not conflict with existing law and need the Governor's previous approval. It covers both judicial and administrative supervision, and the High Court can act suo motu (on its own, without anyone applying)
Control over subordinate courts (Art 235)
Administrative control

Decides posting, promotion, leave and discipline of judicial officers below the rank of district judge; is consulted on the appointment of district judges; its decisions (law) bind the lower courts in its territory
Court of record (Art 215)
Its records are accepted as evidence, and it can punish for contempt (disrespect or disobedience of the court)

Contempt is defined in the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 (civil contempt = disobeying a court order; criminal contempt = acts that lower the court's authority). It can punish contempt of itself and of subordinate courts. It can also review its own judgments, even though no Article says so expressly
Judicial review (Art 13, 226)
Can declare Central or State laws and government orders void if they violate the Constitution

The 42nd Amendment, 1976 (Art 226A) stopped High Courts from testing Central laws; the 43rd Amendment, 1977 restored this power. A High Court can also test the validity of a constitutional amendment under Art 226

blocks.text: Subordinate (lower) courts are the courts below the High Court — the district court and the courts under it. Their provisions are in Part VI, Chapter VI, Articles 233–237. Aim: keep them independent of the executive (government).

blocks.title: Articles at a glance
head: Article
What it says
rows: Art 233

Appointment, posting and promotion of district judges — by the Governor in consultation with the High Court (all three need consultation, not only appointment). A person recruited directly (not by promotion) must: (1) not already be in Central or State government service, (2) have been an advocate or pleader for at least 7 years, and (3) be recommended by the High Court.
Art 233A

Validates (makes legal, with retrospective effect) certain district-judge appointments made before 1966 and the judgments they delivered. Added by the 20th Amendment Act 1966 after the Chandra Mohan case (1966). Only these past appointments — not a blank cheque for future illegal appointments.
Art 234

Recruitment of persons other than district judges (for example Civil Judge, Junior Division) to the State judicial service — by the Governor, after consulting BOTH the State Public Service Commission (SPSC) and the High Court, under rules he frames. In practice the SPSC (or High Court) holds the exam.
Art 235

Control over district courts and courts below them is vested in the High Court — including posting, promotion and grant of leave of judicial officers below district-judge rank. The High Court must still follow the officer's legal service conditions; any appeal right under his service law is not taken away.
Art 236

Definitions. 'District judge' includes: judge of a city civil court, additional, joint and assistant district judge, chief judge of a small cause court, chief presidency magistrate, additional chief presidency magistrate, sessions judge, additional and assistant sessions judge. NOT a tribunal judge. 'Judicial service' means a service made up only of persons meant to fill the post of district judge and civil judicial posts below it.
Art 237
Governor, by public notification, may apply these provisions to any class of magistrates from a date he fixes, with such exceptions and modifications as he specifies (not automatic or uniform).

First the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution, by two-thirds of members present and voting, that it is needed in the national interest. items: Highest judicial authority in the district; the highest criminal court of the district is the Court of Session.

Has judicial AND administrative powers, plus supervision over all lower courts of the district.

Can pass any sentence including life imprisonment and death — but a death sentence must be confirmed by the High Court, whether or not the convict appeals.

blocks.title: Lok Adalat ('People's Court') — features
items: Part of ADR (Alternative Dispute Resolution); based on Gandhian principles; settles disputes by compromise — no winner, no loser.
First Lok Adalat camp after independence: Gujarat, 1982.
Organised by the State Legal Services Authority, District Legal Services Authority, Supreme Court Legal Services Committee, High Court Legal Services Committee or Taluk Legal Services Committee.
Members: serving or retired judicial officers and other persons of the area; usually a judicial officer (chairman), a lawyer and a social worker — so not only judicial officers.
Handles both cases pending in court AND pre-litigation disputes (not yet filed); civil matters and compoundable criminal offences (offences that can be settled between parties).
No jurisdiction over non-compoundable offences.

Pending case referred if: both parties agree, OR one party applies and the court sees a chance of settlement (court must first give the other side a reasonable hearing), OR the court itself finds it fit.
Pre-litigation matter: referred by the organising authority on one party's application.

Has civil-court powers under the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) 1908 for summoning witnesses, documents, affidavit evidence, public records; fixes its own procedure; its proceedings are treated as judicial proceedings.
Its award (decision) is treated as a decree of a civil court; final and binding; NO appeal to any court.
No court fee; fee already paid is refunded if settled.
If no settlement: pending case returns to the referring court and continues from the stage reached before referral; pre-litigation parties are advised to go to court.

subcards.title: Judicial review, activism & PIL
subcards.summary: How courts test laws, when they become active, and how PIL works.
at_a_glance: USA – Marbury v. Madison (1803), Chief Justice John Marshall
Basic feature of the Constitution – cannot be removed even by amendment
Narrower – India has 'procedure established by law', USA 'due process of law'
Began mid-1970s – Justices Krishna Iyer, Bhagwati, Chinnappa Reddy, D.A. Desai
Origin USA (1960s); in India early 1980s; first case Hussainara Khatoon (1979)

blocks.text: Judicial review = the power of the judiciary (Supreme Court AND High Courts) to examine whether laws (legislative enactments) and executive orders of both the Centre and the States agree with the Constitution. If they go against it (ultra vires = beyond the powers given), the court declares them illegal, unconstitutional and invalid (null and void = having no legal effect). The government then cannot enforce them.

blocks.title: Basics
head: Point
Fact
rows: Origin
USA. First stated in Marbury v. Madison (1803) by John Marshall, then Chief Justice of the US Supreme Court. The US Constitution does not mention it in words.
Borrowed from
USA (Indian Constitution borrowed judicial review, independent judiciary and Fundamental Rights from the US). Rule of law – Britain; procedure established by law – Japan.
In India
The Constitution itself gives the power (no need to infer it, unlike USA). The phrase 'judicial review' is NOT used or defined anywhere in the Constitution.
Who has it
Supreme Court and High Courts (not the Supreme Court alone).
Three categories (Justice Syed Shah Mohamed Quadri)

1. Review of constitutional amendments  2. Review of laws of Parliament, State Legislatures and subordinate (delegated) legislation  3. Review of administrative (executive) action of Union, States and authorities
Examples of use

Golaknath (1967), Bank Nationalisation – R.C. Cooper (1970), Privy Purses – Madhav Rao Scindia (1970), Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Minerva Mills (1980), NJAC case (2015: 99th Amendment and NJAC Act struck down)

blocks.title: Why judicial review is needed (3 purposes)
items: To uphold the supremacy of the Constitution (every law must conform to the Constitution).
To maintain federal equilibrium (balance between Centre and States) – so judicial review is called a symbol and feature of a federal government.
To protect the Fundamental Rights of citizens.
NOT a purpose: executive supremacy or legislative supremacy.

blocks.title: Who said what
head: Words
Said by – case
rows: 'In India it is the Constitution that is supreme… it is for the judiciary to decide whether any enactment is constitutional'
Chief Justice Kania – A.K. Gopalan (1950)
Court is the 'sentinel on the qui vive' (watchful guard) of Fundamental Rights
Chief Justice Patanjali Sastri – State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952)
As long as Fundamental Rights exist, judicial review must be available to protect them
Justice Khanna – Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
'This Court is the ultimate interpreter of the Constitution'
Justice Bhagwati – State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977)
Without judicial review, Fundamental Rights become 'a mere adornment' (only decoration); 'rights without remedies are as writ in water' (rights that cannot be enforced are useless)
Chief Justice Y.V. Chandrachud – Minerva Mills (1980)
Judges keep the balance of power; legislature and executive must not cross limits
Chief Justice Ahmadi – L. Chandra Kumar (1997)
Judicial review keeps federal balance and 'adjusts the Constitution to meet new conditions'
Justice Ramaswami – S.S. Bola (1997)

blocks.title: Role & criticism
items: Supreme Court = guardian, custodian and final interpreter of the Constitution. It also has the duty to make constitutional ideals real, including Directive Principles – but it cannot change the Preamble on its own (only Parliament amends).
Criticism – 'counter-majoritarian difficulty': unelected judges can strike down laws made by elected representatives.

blocks.text: The phrase 'judicial review' appears nowhere, but these Articles clearly give the power (Laxmikanth's list).

What it provides

Certificate for appeal to Supreme Court from High Courts (added by 44th Amendment, 1978)
Art 135

Special leave to appeal from any court or tribunal (except military tribunal / court martial)
Art 143
President may seek Supreme Court's opinion on a question of law or fact (advisory) – the US Supreme Court has no advisory role
Art 226
High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights AND 'for any other purpose' (legal rights) – NOT itself a Fundamental Right
Art 227
High Court's superintendence over all courts and tribunals in its territory (except military)
Art 245 and Art 246
Art 245: territorial extent of laws; Art 246: subject matter of laws (Union, State, Concurrent Lists)
Art 251 and Art 254
Conflict between Central and State law – Central law prevails, State law void
Art 372

blocks.title: Key points
items: The Supreme Court mainly exercises judicial review through Art 13 and Art 32; the two provisions that most clearly express it for both courts are Art 32 and Art 226 – also the main routes for PIL and for 'guarding' Fundamental Rights.
There are five writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, quo warranto. 'Injunction' is NOT a constitutional writ.
High Court's writ power is wider than Supreme Court's (Fundamental Rights + 'any other purpose'). The Supreme Court can issue writs only for Fundamental Rights; writs are not limited to appeals.

42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Art 131A (only Supreme Court could decide validity of Central laws) and Art 226A (High Courts could not consider validity of Central laws under Art 226); 43rd Amendment (1977) omitted both. So today a High Court CAN declare a Central law, and even a constitutional amendment, invalid.

Writ jurisdiction of High Courts (Art 226) → see High Courts

blocks.title: Three grounds to challenge a law or executive order
items: (a) it violates Fundamental Rights (Part III);
(b) it is outside the competence (power) of the authority that made it;
(c) it is repugnant to (against) a constitutional provision.

blocks.title: Scope: India vs USA (Kashyap's explanation)
head: Aspect
India
USA
rows: Clause
'Procedure established by law' (Art 21) – borrowed from Japan
'Due process of law'
What court checks
Mainly substantive: is the law within the power of the authority? Not its reasonableness, suitability or policy
Substantive AND procedural – can strike down a law as unreasonable or unfair ('due process' in essence = natural justice / fairness)
Result
Scope NARROWER
Scope WIDER – critics call the US Supreme Court a 'third chamber' / 'super-legislature'
Text
Expressly given by Constitution
Not mentioned in Constitution

blocks.title: Points
items: India = a synthesis of the American principle of judicial supremacy and the British principle of parliamentary supremacy.
Britain: no judicial review; Parliament sovereign. India: Parliament's power is limited by written Constitution, federalism, Fundamental Rights and judicial review (UPSC 2021).
Questions on the validity of amendments / substantial questions of constitutional law are heard by a Constitution Bench (minimum 5 judges, Art 145(3)).
Executive orders, administrative action and delegated legislation (rules under an Act) are all reviewable – a rule beyond its parent Act is struck down as ultra vires.
Spirit of the Constitution = its underlying values; it never allows authorities to ignore explicit constitutional limits.

blocks.title: Doctrines & legal terms
head: Doctrine / term
Meaning
rows: Severability
Only the offending part of a law is void; the valid part survives
Eclipse
A pre-Constitution law inconsistent with Fundamental Rights is dormant (eclipsed), not dead; it revives if the Fundamental Rights bar is removed
Waiver
A citizen cannot give up (waive) Fundamental Rights
Pith and substance
The true nature of a law decides competence; incidental touching of another List does not invalidate it
Ultra vires
Beyond the powers given by law
Null and void
Having no legal effect
Locus standi
Right or entitlement of a person to approach the court
Suo motu
Court acting on its own motion
Amicus curiae
'Friend of the court' – assists the court
Epistolary jurisdiction
Treating a letter or postcard as a writ petition
Res judicata
A matter finally decided cannot be reopened by the same parties
Proportionality
A restriction must not go beyond what its aim needs

Validity of proceedings in State Legislature

blocks.title: Legislature & contempt
items: Keshav Singh case (Special Reference 1964): legislative privilege is not an absolute bar – a High Court can hear a habeas corpus (production of body) petition of a non-member jailed by the Assembly for contempt.

Contempt power (Art 129 and Art 215): wilful disobedience of court orders and scandalising the court are contempt. Activism needs this power, but contempt does not exist merely because of activism (separate ideas).

blocks.title: Response to an unwelcome judgment
items: If the Government or Parliament dislikes a Supreme Court decision, it can (1) pass a constitutional amendment, or (2) enact a validating law that removes the legal basis of the judgment – it cannot simply ignore the decision or change judges.
A validating law cannot directly overrule a judgment; it must change the law on which the judgment rested.

sections.heading: Judicial review as a basic feature (and the Ninth Schedule)

blocks.text: The Supreme Court holds judicial review a 'basic feature' (part of the basic structure). So even a constitutional amendment, or an ordinary law, cannot take it away. The Constitution itself does not define 'basic structure' – the courts developed it (UPSC 2020).

Basic features: limited amending power, judicial review, and balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles (DPSPs)
Waman Rao case (1980)
Ninth Schedule laws added after 24 April 1973 valid only if they do not damage basic structure
Fixed 24 April 1973 (Kesavananda judgment date) as the cut-off date
P. Sambamurthy case (1986)
Struck down the proviso to Art 371D(5), which let the State Government modify or cancel orders of the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal
Rule of law, judicial review
S.P. Sampath Kumar case (1986)
Administrative tribunals accepted as effective substitutes for High Courts in service matters
Later corrected (overruled on this point) by L. Chandra Kumar (1997)
Kihoto Hollohan case (1992)
Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law), which barred courts from defection cases, held invalid; the Speaker's decision on defection can be reviewed by courts
Judicial review of anti-defection rulings
S.R. Bommai case (1994)
9-judge bench: President's Rule proclamations under Art 356 can be reviewed by courts; secularism and federalism are basic features
Landmark on President's Rule
L. Chandra Kumar case (1997)

Judicial review by High Courts (Art 226 and 227) and by the Supreme Court (Art 32) is part of the basic structure. The clauses Art 323A(2)(d) and Art 323B(3)(d), which excluded courts, are invalid. An appeal against a tribunal order goes first to a Division Bench (2 or more judges) of the High Court
Tribunals cannot bypass the High Court
I.R. Coelho case (2007)
No blanket immunity for Ninth Schedule laws; laws added after 24 April 1973 can be tested against Art 14, 15, 19, 21 and basic structure ('rights test', 'impact test')
Ninth Schedule review
Madras Bar Association case (2014)
Struck down the National Tax Tribunal Act, 2005
High Court review power protected
NJAC case – SC Advocates-on-Record Association (2015)
Struck down 99th Amendment & NJAC Act, 2014
Independence of judiciary = basic feature
Rojer Mathew case (2019)
Struck down the Tribunal Rules, 2017 (made under Section 184 of the Finance Act, 2017) on appointment and service conditions of tribunal members; decided 13 Nov 2019
Tribunal independence
Madras Bar Association case (19 Nov 2025)

Struck down key provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 – minimum age of 50 years for appointment, fixed 4-year tenure, and the selection committee recommending 2 names per vacancy – as violating judicial independence; Parliament cannot re-enact provisions already struck down
Latest tribunal ruling (as of Nov 2026)

blocks.title: Basics
head: Point
Fact
rows: Meaning

Proactive role of the judiciary to protect citizens' rights and promote justice; forcing legislature and executive to do their constitutional duties. 'Voluntary intervention by the judiciary in public interest'.
Also called
Judicial dynamism. Opposite (antithesis) = judicial restraint (self-control).
Origin
USA. Term coined 1947 by Arthur Schlesinger Jr. (US historian) in the article 'The Supreme Court: 1947' in Fortune magazine.
In India
Mid-1970s – Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer, P.N. Bhagwati, O. Chinnappa Reddy, D.A. Desai (NOT the 1990s, NOT Britain)
Basis
No separate Article – it is a way of using the power of judicial review. Calling a judgment 'activist' gives the court no extra power; it must still find a legal power for every order.
Two aspects in India
(i) Directions to authorities to protect rights / public interest – PIL falls here; (ii) Expansive interpretation of Fundamental Rights – Art 14, 19, 21
Judicial pessimism
Interpreting law without trying to enhance its beneficial (social) aspects
Judicial adventurism / overreach
Activism crossing limits into the domain of other organs (for example, continuously running administration) – threatens separation of powers

blocks.title: Judicial review vs judicial activism
items: Review = interpreting law in light of the Constitution; activism = moulding law to suit changing social and economic needs so constitutional ideals become real.
Activism is that form of review in which judges also apply policy preferences ('judicial legislation').
Expanded locus standi through PIL widened judicial review – critics named this 'judicial activism'.

blocks.title: Dr. B.L. Wadehra – five reasons for activism
head: Wadehra's reason
Explanation
rows: Near collapse of responsible government
Legislature and executive fail in their functions
Citizens look to judiciary
For protection of rights and freedoms
Judicial enthusiasm
Judges wish to take part in social reform; encourages PIL, liberal locus standi
Legislative vacuum
Unlegislated areas – courts fill the gap
Constitutional scheme
Constitution itself gives courts scope to play an active role
blocks.note: Never: 'unlimited authority to disregard constitutional limits'.

blocks.title: Subhash Kashyap – six eventualities when courts may step in
items: Legislature fails its responsibilities
'Hung' legislature – weak, insecure government avoids decisions
Those in power refer hard issues to courts to delay or pass the blame
Legislature and executive fail to protect basic rights (decent life, healthy surroundings, honest administration)
Courts misused by a strong authoritarian party government (as during the Emergency)
Courts' own weakness for populism, publicity, headlines

blocks.title: Activators of judicial activism (Upendra Baxi)
items: Upendra Baxi listed 15 activator groups: civil rights; people's rights; consumer rights; bonded labour; citizens for environmental action; groups against large irrigation projects; rights of child; custodial rights; poverty rights; indigenous peoples' rights; women's rights; Bar-based (autonomy/accountability of judiciary); media autonomy (State-owned media); assorted lawyer-based groups; assorted individual petitioners. (Not legislature parties; not 'only registered environmental bodies'.)

Activism
Restraint

Proactive; can mould law for social change

blocks.title: Six US assumptions of judicial restraint (all except no. 2 hold in India)
head: US assumption
Content
rows: 1. Undemocratic court
Non-elected, so should defer to democratic branches
2. Questionable origin of judicial review
Not expressly granted by US Constitution – does NOT hold in India (expressly given by Art 13, 32, 226)
3. Separation of powers
Each organ stays in its own sphere; policy left to legislature and executive
4. Federalism
Defer to actions of state governments
5. Pragmatic
Court depends on Congress and public acceptance, so must not overstep
6. Aristocratic
As custodian of legal tradition, court should not descend into politics

blocks.title: Supreme Court's call for restraint (2007)
head: Point
Detail
rows: Case
Divisional Manager, Aravali Golf Club v. Chander Hass (6 December 2007)
Facts
Courts had directed creating a tractor-driver post that was never sanctioned and regularising workers – held beyond jurisdiction
Observations

Judges must not run the government or 'behave like emperors'; activism must not become 'judicial adventurism'; quoted Montesquieu's 'The Spirit of Laws' on overreach; courts lack administrative expertise and resources; remedy for bad government is the ballot
Restraint & independence
Restraint respects equality of the three branches and protects judicial independence – encroachment makes voters and politicians demand closer monitoring of judges

blocks.title: Basics
head: Point
Fact
rows: Origin
USA, 1960s – legal representation for unrepresented groups (poor, environmentalists, consumers, minorities)
In India
Introduced early 1980s; first case Hussainara Khatoon (1979). Seeds: Mumbai Kamgar Sabha v. Abdulbhai (1976, Krishna Iyer); liberal standing: S.P. Gupta (1981, Bhagwati)
Pioneers

Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer and Justice P.N. Bhagwati. Bhagwati later became Chief Justice (1985–86); Krishna Iyer never became Chief Justice. When PIL began (1979–81) the Chief Justice of India was Y.V. Chandrachud (1978–85); Bhagwati was then a puisne (ordinary) judge – but exam keys name Bhagwati as the judge who introduced PIL
Link
A product and the most popular form of judicial activism (NOT of judicial restraint)
Other names
Social Action Litigation (SAL), Social Interest Litigation (SIL), Class Action Litigation (CAL)
Routes

Art 32 (Supreme Court) and Art 226 (High Court). In High Court, a PIL can also enforce legal rights, not only Fundamental Rights. Related: Art 39A (free legal aid), Section 133 CrPC – now Section 152 BNSS (magistrate removes public nuisance)
Key innovation

Relaxation of the traditional rule of locus standi (normally only the injured person can sue). Any public-spirited citizen or social organisation with 'sufficient interest' can sue for those who are poor, ignorant or disadvantaged – no personal loss needed
Supreme Court definition

'A legal action initiated in a court of law for the enforcement of public interest or general interest in which the public or a class of the community have pecuniary interest or some interest by which their legal rights or liabilities are affected'
Purposes
Vindicate the rule of law; access to justice for weaker sections; meaningful realisation of Fundamental Rights

blocks.title: Features of PIL
items: Strategic arm of the legal aid movement – justice for poor masses.
Not adversarial (not party vs party); promotes public interest, not one individual's right.
Co-operative effort of petitioner, State/public authority and court.
Redresses public injury, enforces public duty, protects diffused collective rights.
Court is assertive and creative; can appoint commissions to find facts.
Procedure is flexible but must still be a judicial procedure (fairness and proof remain).
No adjudication of individual rights.

blocks.title: Principles of PIL – Guruvayur Devaswom Managing Committee v. C.K. Rajan (2003)
items: Court can entertain a petition under Art 32 and Art 226 from anyone interested in the welfare of disadvantaged people.
A letter or telegram can be treated as a PIL (epistolary jurisdiction); procedural rules and pleadings relaxed.
Court invokes Art 14, 21 and international human-rights conventions where injustice is done to many.
Once satisfied prima facie (at first sight), the State may not be allowed to object to maintainability.
Res judicata: whether it applies depends on the nature of the petition and the facts of the case.
A purely private dispute between warring groups cannot be a PIL – but if a private case reveals a wider public problem, the court may inquire into it in the interest of justice.
Court may appoint commissions or bodies to investigate facts and even manage a public institution.
Court will not ordinarily enter policy (unless policy is illegal or unconstitutional) and will stay within known areas of judicial review.
A High Court has no power like Art 142, and ordinarily should not entertain a PIL questioning the validity of a statute.

blocks.title: Misuse of PIL
items: Misuse labels: 'Publicity', 'Politics', 'Private', 'Paisa' (money) and 'Middle-class' Interest Litigation – a genuine PIL by a middle-class person is still allowed.
BALCO Employees Union (2001): 'PIL is not a pill or a panacea for all wrongs.'
Janata Dal v. H.S. Chowdhary (1992, Bofors): strangers/busybodies have no standing to intervene in a criminal case.
Ashok Kumar Pandey v. State of West Bengal (2003): PIL must be used with great care, not for personal or political motives.

blocks.title: Guidelines to check misuse – State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal (2010)

steps.step: Each High Court frames proper PIL rules
steps.detail: not each judge with his own procedure

steps.step: Check correctness of contents prima facie
Be satisfied that substantial public interest is involved
Give priority to larger public interest, gravity, urgency
Ensure no personal gain, private or oblique motive

blocks.title: Applying it
items: Reject a 'PIL' filed for personal or business rivalry, private vendetta, publicity or political mileage – and impose costs. A social organisation's petition for bonded labourers is genuine.

blocks.text: Article 21 expansion in detail → see Fundamental Rights

items: The phrase 'judicial review' is not used or defined anywhere in the Constitution – yet it is expressly conferred (Art 13, 32, 226…).
Both Supreme Court and High Courts have judicial review; a High Court can strike down a Central law and even a constitutional amendment (Art 131A, 226A omitted by 43rd Amendment, 1977).
Judicial review, judicial activism and PIL all originated in the USA – not Britain.
India's scope is NARROWER than USA (procedure established by law vs due process).
Judicial review is a basic feature – cannot be curtailed by an ordinary law or even an amendment.
Art 32 is a Fundamental Right; Art 226 is not – but Art 226 writ power is wider.
PIL = product of judicial ACTIVISM; pioneers Krishna Iyer & Bhagwati; first case Hussainara Khatoon (1979). Bhagwati (not Krishna Iyer) became Chief Justice of India.
Dates: Marbury 1803; 'activism' 1947 (Schlesinger); activism in India mid-1970s; Aravali Golf Club 2007; Coelho 2007 (cut-off 24 April 1973).
